short: Won the throne in civil war and built the machinery that made the emperor supreme.
full:
Prince Ōama took the throne in 673 after defeating his nephew, Emperor Kōbun, in the Jinshin War of the previous year — the largest internal conflict of ancient Japan, fought over the succession to Tenji. Having won by force, Tenmu ruled without appointing a chancellor and filled the senior offices with his own sons, keeping the great clans out of the centre of government in a way no earlier sovereign had managed.

His reign gave the institution much of its later shape. The title tennō, heavenly sovereign, and the name Nihon for the country both came into settled use under him. He ordered the compilation of a legal code, completed after his death as the Asuka Kiyomihara and then the Taihō codes; reorganised the clan titles into eight ranks dependent on the throne; and commanded the compilation of the imperial chronicles that became the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. He died in 686 and was succeeded by his widow, Empress Jitō.
